extracted.intended_audience: readers or travellers interested in nineteenth-century Saharan travel and practical advice for interacting with Touarick society
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and using a nineteenth‑century first‑person travel narrative about Ghat and Touarick society; useful for travellers, historians, or readers of travel literature seeking practical cultural/behavioral guidance embedded in the account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give handsome presents to local sheikhs
rubrics_metrics.description: Send an appropriately generous present to Sheikhs; a small or inappropriate gift may offend and be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative: the author was advised by the Governor to 'by all means' send a handsome present to Khanouhen; a broken loaf of sugar and trifling items caused Khanouhen to return the present in rage. Practical fix: supply money or increase the value (the author ultimately gave five or six dollars; later eight dollars to another Sheikh). Also note that Touarick ladies expect items (cloves, beads, looking-glasses) and will request more; the Touaricks 'will take everything you offer them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer money when goods will offend or be inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: When gifts of goods risk offense or are rejected, offering money (the cash equivalent) can pacify a dissatisfied Sheikh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Khanouhen returned the goods; Bel-Kasem advised giving 'ten dollars in money' or the value in cash to satisfy him. The author sent cash and the dispute was settled while leaving the other goods for the ladies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect extreme slowness in Souk/merchant transactions ('be-shwaiah')
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial dealings proceed very slowly; transactions that would take days in Europe take weeks or months in the Souk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'The Souk of Ghat... A month usually passes before the Souk opens, and six weeks more are consumed before a merchant can or will get off.' The text illustrates stepwise delays (heard of a slave, talked about next day, searched out the day after, etc.) and the phrase 'be-shwaiah, be-shwaiah' ('by little and by little'). Travelers/merchants should not expect prompt business and must budget long delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring patience and conciliation as essential equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Patience and a conciliatory manner are necessary to endure insults, pestering visitors, and general social frictions in Saharan towns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author admonition: 'To bear all this... requires, as Mr. Fletcher hints, "Conciliation," with an occasional dose, I should think, of that most necessary of all Saharan equipments... PATIENCE.' Examples: being hooted by rabble, repeated begging, and frequent intrusive visits that are only mollified by small presents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make formal complaints against Touaricks — use caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints against Touaricks are unlikely to be welcomed and may worsen relations; discretion is often the safer course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: the incident of Ouweek was 'entirely smuggled up, and never even alluded to by the Sultan or Khanouhen.' The author notes Touaricks (even Sheikhs) are displeased when complaints are made; 'Shafou... always told me, "My people will be as kind to you as I am," and would not hear of complaints.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local patrons/hosts for safe travel and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Securing the protection or patronage of a powerful local (e.g., a marabout or Sheikh) enables safer passage and access to distant regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jabour (a marabout Sheikh) guaranteed that 'With a slave of Jabour... you may go to Timbuctoo, and all parts of Sahara.' The author was promised the Prince's protection for travel if he decided to go to Timbuctoo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose routes advised by locals; avoid known dangerous passes
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow local route advice for safety; prefer safer alternative routes when reports indicate banditry or skirmishes on certain roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific advice: 'Go to Soudan, there's not much sickness, go viâ Aheer. The road viâ Bornou is not safe now.' The recommendation is based on recent skirmishes and local intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and navigate local gift/tribute politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts and tribute are entangled with local rivalries; failing to account for factional jealousies among Sheikhs can produce political problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes jealousies among many Sheikhs over Souk presents: 'A burning jealousy rankles... Each wishes to be the greater man, in order to have more presents.' There is a three‑faction classification (Monarchical, Aristocratic, Democratic) — knowing who is allied to whom (e.g., Khanouhen, Shafou, the Governor, Jabour, Berka) helps decide whom to treat and how to present gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visitors and lower‑class locals expect small offerings; failing to give is insulting
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, frequent gifts or food are expected by many visitors; not providing them is taken as an insult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author: 'Every visitor who leaves me, without a small present, however trifling it may be, considers himself insulted by me, or that I don't like him.' Practical implication: keep a supply of small items (dates, sugar, peas, tobacco, etc.) to placate the rabble and avoid daily friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe food‑sharing and hospitality norms (do not take strangers' food)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are strict local customs around who may share whose food; for example, Touaricks decline to eat a stranger's cuscasou.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example conversation: Sidi Omer refuses the author's cuscasou, saying 'The Touaricks must not eat the cuscasou of strangers... You ought to eat my cuscasou.' Travelers should respect such hospitality taboos and not impose food sharing contrary to local norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slave‑labour economy: expect in‑kind wages and informal property norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Day labour and slave labour are commonly compensated in grain, dates, or in‑kind rations rather than cash; notions of personal property are flexible under economic pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: 'A slave will have about a quarter of a peck of barley, or other grain, given him for a day's work... Corn and ghusub are given to day‑labourers instead of money.' Anecdote: a butcher's division by 'pieces of wood' and a slave carrying off most of the meat illustrate ad hoc and culturally specific practices; travelers/employers should be aware of these norms to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of local verbal/performative displays and potential threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Strange or solemn vocalizations, ostensible prayers, or ritualized phrases may accompany begging, intimidation, or social performance — interpret context carefully and exercise caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incident: two figures in the dark recited 'There is no God but God, and Mahomet is the prophet of God' and another chanted 'Bor-nou-se! Bor-nou-se!' — the author feared an attack but realized it resembled begging or intimidation. Travelers should be alert and pragmatic in assessing such displays (retreating when servants absent, avoiding direct confrontation).
